plan.title: Everyday Probability: Chance & Evidence
plan.hook: Most probability mistakes are not arithmetic mistakes — they are setup mistakes: the wrong outcomes counted, the overlap counted twice, or the wrong denominator under the fraction.
objectives: List a sample space and identify events as subsets before computing any probability
Apply the union rule with its overlap subtraction, and multiply for independent events joined by "and"
Judge a positive test by the share of true positives among all positives, using the base rate
prerequisites: None — starts from everyday experience with dice and counts

sections.heading: Define the possible outcomes first
points: Before computing a probability, list the outcomes that count — the sample space
On a fair six-sided die the sample space is {1,2,3,4,5,6} and events are subsets of it
"Even and greater than four" is the single outcome {6}, so its probability is 1/6

sections.heading: “And” and “or” use different rules
points: For "or", add the probabilities and subtract the overlap so the shared part is counted once
For independent events joined by "and", multiply the probabilities
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); independence is what licenses the multiplication

sections.heading: Choose the right denominator
points: A positive test is not the same as the true-positive rate among all items
Of 1,000 parts with 10 defective, the test flags 108 positives: 9 true and 99 false
So a positive is truly defective only 9/108 ≈ 8.3% of the time — condition on the positives, the evidence you actually have

questions.q: What must you write down before computing any probability in this course?
questions.hint: The section heading gives the order of operations.
questions.answer: The outcomes that count — the sample space. On a fair six-sided die it is {1,2,3,4,5,6}, and every event is a subset of that space.

questions.q: On a fair die, what is the probability of "even and greater than four", and why?
questions.hint: List the outcomes that satisfy both descriptions at once.
questions.answer: The evens are {2,4,6} and the outcomes greater than four are {5,6}; their intersection is only {6}, so the probability is 1/6.

sections.heading: “And” and “or” use different rules
sections.body: Union adds probabilities and subtracts the overlap. Independent conjunction multiplies.
sections.visual: The shared part of the two sets must be counted once for “or.”

questions.q: Why does the union rule subtract the overlap?
questions.hint: Picture the shared part of the two sets being counted twice.
questions.answer: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the shared part, A∩B, twice. Subtracting P(A and B) makes the shared part count once for "or".

questions.q: When are you allowed to multiply probabilities for an "and"?
questions.hint: The rule names a condition on how the events relate.
questions.answer: When the events are independent. Independent conjunction multiplies: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

sections.heading: Choose the right denominator
sections.body: A positive test is not the same as a true positive rate among all items.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 800 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Among positive tests, choose the right denominator"><title>Among positive tests, choose the right denominator</title><rect x="0" y="0" width="800" height="400" rx="16" fill="#101923"/><text x="28" y="35" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="21" font-family="sans-serif">Among positive tests, choose the right denominator</text><path d="M28 51 L772 51" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="120" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="16">1,000 parts · 10 defective</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="170" fill="#7ee2a8" font-size="16">9 true positives · 99 false positives</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="220" fill="#ffd479" font-size="16">108 total positives</text></g><g class="lw-step"><text x="80" y="280" fill="#e8ecf1" font-size="20">9 / 108 ≈ 8.3% truly defective</text></g><rect x="480" y="110" width="250" height="180" rx="12" fill="#172331" stroke="#344253"/><text x="500" y="150" fill="#ffd479" font-size="16">Not 9/10</text><text x="500" y="190" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="14">Condition on the</text><text x="500" y="215" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="14">evidence you have</text><text x="500" y="255" fill="#7cc7ff" font-size="14">Denominator = positives</text><path d="M28 350 L772 350" fill="none" stroke="#344253" stroke-width="2"/><text x="28" y="379" fill="#9aa6b8" font-size="15">Base rates change the meaning of a positive test</text></svg>

questions.q: A test flags 108 parts as positive, and 9 of those are truly defective. What does a positive result actually tell you?
questions.hint: Choose the denominator the diagram insists on.
questions.answer: That the part is truly defective with probability 9/108 ≈ 8.3%. The denominator is all the positives — the evidence you have — not the 10 defective parts overall.

questions.q: Why is "9 out of 10 defectives were caught" the wrong headline for this test?
questions.hint: It conditions on being defective; you hold a positive result, not a defective part.
questions.answer: Because you never observe "defective" directly — you observe a positive test. Among positives, most (99 of 108) are false positives, so the base rate changes the meaning of a positive result.

questions.q: On a fair six-sided die, the probability of rolling "even and greater than four" is…
questions.explain: The sample space is {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Even outcomes are {2,4,6}; outcomes greater than four are {5,6}. Their intersection is the single outcome {6}, so the probability is 1/6.

choices: Any single roll of the die
A subset of the sample space
A probability greater than one half
questions.explain: Events are subsets of the sample space: "even" is the subset {2,4,6} of {1,2,3,4,5,6}. You define the outcomes first, then pick out the subsets that count.

questions.q: P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4, with P(A and B) = 0.2. What is P(A or B)?
questions.explain: Union adds the probabilities and subtracts the overlap: 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. Adding without subtracting counts the shared part twice.

questions.q: Two independent events have probabilities 0.5 and 0.2. The probability that both happen is…
questions.explain: Independent conjunction multiplies: 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1. Adding would be the (overlap-uncorrected) union move, not the "and" rule for independent events.

questions.q: Of 1,000 parts, 10 are defective. A test returns 108 positives, of which 9 are true positives. A part tests positive. The chance it is actually defective is about…
questions.explain: Condition on the evidence you have: the denominator is the 108 positives, so 9/108 ≈ 8.3%. The tempting 9/10 conditions on defectives, which is not what a positive result shows you.

questions.q: The 99 false positives in this example matter because…
choices: They show the test is useless
They outnumber true positives among the positives, so a positive is usually false
They change the number of defective parts
They make the base rate irrelevant
questions.explain: Among the 108 positives, 99 are false and only 9 are true — so a positive result is usually a false alarm. That is the base rate changing the meaning of a positive test.

sections.title: Define the outcomes first
bullets: The sample space lists every outcome that counts: {1,2,3,4,5,6} for a fair die.
Events are subsets of the sample space.
"Even and greater than four" is just {6} — probability 1/6.
sections.notes: Every error later in the course comes from skipping this step. Write the outcomes down, mark the subsets, and only then divide counts.
sections.visual: On a fair six-sided die, {2, 4, 6} are even and {5, 6} are greater than four. Their intersection contains only 6, so the chance of “even and greater than four” is 1/6.

sections.title: "Or" adds and corrects; "and" multiplies
bullets: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
The subtraction stops the overlap being counted twice.
sections.notes: A union is a merged set: add both sides, then remove the double-counted middle. A conjunction of independent events is a path: multiply along it. The words "or" and "and" pick different rules.
sections.visual: The shared part of the two sets must be counted once for “or.”

sections.title: Condition on the evidence you have
bullets: A positive means truly defective only 9/108 ≈ 8.3% of the time.
The denominator is the positives — not the defectives.
sections.notes: A positive test feels like a verdict, but it is evidence, and weak evidence when false positives swamp true ones. Always ask: out of all results like this one, how many are real?

enrichment.audioTitle: Everyday Probability: Chance & Evidence — a conversation

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Before any formula: a fair die. What is the sample space, and what is the event "even and greater than four"?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: The sample space is {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Even is {2,4,6}, greater than four is {5,6} — the overlap is just {6}.

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: One outcome out of six: 1/6. The trick was listing outcomes before computing.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That ordering is the course's first rule. Now "or": P(A) is 0.5, P(B) is 0.4. Is P(A or B) simply 0.9?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Only if they never overlap. Otherwise the shared part is counted twice, so subtract P(A and B).

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: If the events are independent, multiply. Independence is the condition that licenses it.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Good. Last setup: 1,000 parts, 10 defective. A test produces 108 positives, 9 of them true. A part tests positive — how confident are you that it is defective?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: The test caught 9 of 10 defectives, so about 90%?

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: That is the denominator trap. You are holding a positive, not a defective. Among the 108 positives, how many are real?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Nine. So 9 out of 108 — about 8.3%. The other 99 positives are false.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: Exactly. Why does the intuitive 90% feel so right?

turns.speaker: student
turns.line: Because it conditions on the defectives, the group I cannot observe. I have to condition on the evidence I actually have — the positives.

turns.speaker: teacher
turns.line: And that is the base rate doing its work: rare conditions make even good tests produce mostly false positives.

nodes.label: Everyday Probability: Chance & Evidence
nodes.note: Set up the count honestly — the right outcomes, the overlap once, and the denominator you actually observe.

nodes.label: Sample space first
nodes.note: List the outcomes that count; events are subsets of that space.

nodes.label: Intersection picks both
nodes.note: "Even and greater than four" on a die is the single outcome {6}, probability 1/6.

nodes.label: And vs or
nodes.note: Union adds and subtracts the overlap; independent conjunction multiplies.

nodes.label: The right denominator
nodes.note: Judge evidence against all results like it: 9 true positives among 108 positives is ≈ 8.3%.

nodes.label: Base rates rule positives
nodes.note: When the condition is rare, false positives can outnumber true ones, changing what a positive means.
